chapter: First bands and New Orleans style
title: Traditional rhythm versus Dixieland: two-beat bass drum
summary: He explains that trumpeters rested, drummers kept a single parade beat until the last chorus, and four beats came with Dixieland.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Did the, I mean music, when you were coming out, was it the same sort of thing as now? I mean the trumpet would just play a couple of choruses in the lead, and then they'd take solos? No, no, they didn't do that.

See back in there, most of the trumpet would take down just for a few balls and wipe his lip, and he would play. But if he would get tired, the clarinet player would take a chorus and let him rest up his lip. But most of them, they were playing all the time. And the beat on the drum was different, back in the traditional music. They didn't hit that four beat, they didn't use that until the very last chorus when they were going out. What do you mean on the bass drum? As they played, they used, we used to call that a single beat. That's the same beat that you hear in a parade. That's the beat, that's traditional playing. And you just couldn't jump in anybody's band in those days and start beating four, four-four times. That came in with Dixaland music. Dixaland came from traditional New Orleans music.
Oh you mean they would play two beats in a measure on the bass drum?

Yeah, they'd make two beats. And they'd hit licks in there now, just like you hear the parade. That's why you hear the parade. But on the lads, whoever was leading the band, they'd stomp their feet and then they would go out. Then the bass would jump on four too, because the bass wasn't playing four all the way through, like in Dixaland. The bass would jump on four beats. And the drum, he would start all four, but he'd always hit a bass lick with the cymbal, like somebody clapping their hands. But not on the beat, after the beat. That was real traditional music. It had a tendency to move you. You even make a little baby feel like dancing. You know, hold on. But when Dixaland music came out, it came out putting four beats and playing plenty of bass music. You see? The fellas jumped all around with the instruments and showing themselves. But traditional jazz, they didn't do that. You know, you played, it's like I told you, you always played one beat until the last going out. Now the difference in the way of the playing, when you were playing Dixaland music, there was plenty of bass music and now and then you'd put a slow number in there or blues. But traditional jazz was more of a, it's called a fast track tempo. And now and then they would play a bass number or a slow number, a bogey bogey. It was most of them, it was moderate, most of them. Most of the tempo all the time was moderate. Or we used to call that a box track.
